claim: Tuft cells emerge within Krt5+ dysplastic regions after influenza injury in murine lungs.
source: We recently described the emergence of tuft cells within Krt5+ dysplastic regions after influenza injury.
evidence: Supported by prior published work from the authors' group and confirmed by immunostaining data in Figure 1A showing tuft cells in dysplastic regions.

claim: Multiple distinct tuft cell populations arise following influenza clearance.
source: Using bulk and single-cell transcriptomics, we characterized and delineated multiple distinct tuft cell populations that arise following influenza clearance.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-Seq data showing distinct clusters in Figure 2A-D.

claim: IL-25 signaling is not required to drive tuft cell development in dysplastic/injured lungs.
source: Distinct from intestinal tuft cells which rely on Type 2 immune signals for their expansion, neither IL-25 nor IL-4ra signaling are required to drive tuft cell development in dysplastic/injured lungs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Il25-/- mice showing no significant difference in tuft cell numbers (Figure 3M-O).

claim: IL-4ra signaling is not required to drive tuft cell development in dysplastic/injured lungs.
source: Distinct from intestinal tuft cells which rely on Type 2 immune signals for their expansion, neither IL-25 nor IL-4ra signaling are required to drive tuft cell development in dysplastic/injured lungs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Il4ra-/- mice showing no significant difference in tuft cell numbers (Figure 3I-K).

claim: Tuft cell expansion occurred independently of type I interferon signaling.
source: In addition, tuft cell expansion occurred independently of type I or type III interferon signaling.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Ifnar-/- mice showing no significant difference in tuft cell numbers (Figure 4D-F).

claim: Tuft cell expansion occurred independently of type III interferon signaling.
source: In addition, tuft cell expansion occurred independently of type I or type III interferon signaling.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Il28r-/- mice showing no significant difference in tuft cell numbers (Figure 4A-C).

claim: Tuft cells were observed upon bleomycin injury.
source: Furthermore, tuft cells were also observed upon bleomycin injury, suggesting that their development may be a general response to severe lung injury.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing Dclk1+ cells in bleomycin-treated mice (Figure 4G).

claim: Tuft cell development may be a general response to severe lung injury.
source: Furthermore, tuft cells were also observed upon bleomycin injury, suggesting that their development may be a general response to severe lung injury.
evidence: Based on observation of tuft cells in both influenza and bleomycin injury models.

claim: In tuft cell deficient mice, Krt5+ dysplasia still occurs.
source: While intestinal tuft cells promote growth and differentiation of surrounding epithelial cells, in the lungs of tuft cell deficient mice, Krt5+ dysplasia still occurs, goblet cell production is unchanged, and there remains no appreciable contribution of Krt5+ cells into more regionally appropriate alveolar Type 2 cells.
evidence: Supported by data in Pou2f3-/- mice showing no significant difference in Krt5+ area (Figure 3A-D).

claim: In tuft cell deficient mice, goblet cell production is unchanged.
source: While intestinal tuft cells promote growth and differentiation of surrounding epithelial cells, in the lungs of tuft cell deficient mice, Krt5+ dysplasia still occurs, goblet cell production is unchanged, and there remains no appreciable contribution of Krt5+ cells into more regionally appropriate alveolar Type 2 cells.
evidence: Supported by Agr2 and Muc5b staining data showing no significant difference in goblet cell markers in Pou2f3-/- mice (Figure 5A-N).

claim: In tuft cell deficient mice, there remains no appreciable contribution of Krt5+ cells into alveolar Type 2 cells.
source: While intestinal tuft cells promote growth and differentiation of surrounding epithelial cells, in the lungs of tuft cell deficient mice, Krt5+ dysplasia still occurs, goblet cell production is unchanged, and there remains no appreciable contribution of Krt5+ cells into more regionally appropriate alveolar Type 2 cells.
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data showing no overlap between Krt5 lineage and SPC+ cells in Pou2f3-/- mice (Figure 6B-D).

claim: The lung exhibits a remarkable capacity for repair following damage induced by pathogen infection.
source: The lung exhibits a remarkable capacity for repair following damage induced by either pathogen infection (e.g., influenza [Kumar et al., 2011], SARS-CoV-2 [Fang et al., 2020]) or sterile injury (e.g., pneumonectomy [Ding et al., 2011], bleomycin [Cong et al., 2020]).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The lung exhibits a remarkable capacity for repair following sterile injury.
source: The lung exhibits a remarkable capacity for repair following damage induced by either pathogen infection (e.g., influenza [Kumar et al., 2011], SARS-CoV-2 [Fang et al., 2020]) or sterile injury (e.g., pneumonectomy [Ding et al., 2011], bleomycin [Cong et al., 2020]).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Normally quiescent tissue-resident alveolar Type 2 cells can self-renew and differentiate into alveolar Type 1 cells upon mild injury.
source: Within the gas-exchanging alveoli, normally quiescent tissue-resident alveolar Type 2 cells (AT2s) can self-renew and differentiate into alveolar Type 1 cells (AT1s) upon mild injury, providing a source of oxygen-exchanging epithelium for effective repair (Barkauskas et al., 2013; Evans et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Upon severe lung injury caused by H1N1 influenza infection, large regions of alveolar epithelium can be ablated.
source: However, upon severe lung injury, for example, that caused by H1N1 influenza infection, large regions of alveolar epithelium can be ablated.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of influenza pathology.

claim: Dysplastic tissue composed of cytokeratin 5 (Krt5)+ p63+ 'basal-like' cells arises after severe influenza injury.
source: In its place, dysplastic tissue arises composed of cytokeratin 5 (Krt5)+ p63+ 'basal-like' cells, forming 'epithelial scars' that appear to provide a short-term benefit in restoring barrier function.
evidence: Based on prior published work and observations.

claim: Dysplastic Krt5+ cells rarely differentiate into AT2s or AT1s capable of gas exchange.
source: However, these cells rarely differentiate into AT2s or AT1s capable of gas exchange (Fernanda de Mello Costa et al., 2020; Vaughan et al., 2015; Xi et al., 2017; Zuo et al., 2015), so dysplastic repair processes may prioritize rapid barrier restoration at the expense of proper lung function.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Dysplastic repair processes may prioritize rapid barrier restoration at the expense of proper lung function.
source: However, these cells rarely differentiate into AT2s or AT1s capable of gas exchange (Fernanda de Mello Costa et al., 2020; Vaughan et al., 2015; Xi et al., 2017; Zuo et al., 2015), so dysplastic repair processes may prioritize rapid barrier restoration at the expense of proper lung function.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that dysplastic cells restore barrier function but do not differentiate into gas-exchanging cells.

claim: Tuft cells are rare cells at homeostasis and were discovered over 50 years ago by electron microscopy.
source: Tuft cells, which depending on their anatomic location, are also known as brush cells (trachea), microvillus cells (olfactory epithelium), or solitary chemosensory cells (sinonasal respiratory epithelium), are rare cells at homeostasis and were discovered over 50 years ago by electron microscopy based on their unique morphology in the rodent gastrointestinal tract and airway (Billipp et al., 2021; Jarvi and Keyrilainen, 1956; Rhodin and Dalhamn, 1956).
evidence: Supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: Tuft cells are non-ciliated epithelial cells that exhibit a bottle-shaped morphology with apical microvilli.
source: Tuft cells are non-ciliated epithelial cells that exhibit a bottle-shaped morphology with apical microvilli that extend into the lumen of mucosal organs (Rhodin and Dalhamn, 1956; Schneider et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Expression profiling of murine intestinal tuft cells suggested that tuft cells have a role in chemosensory, immune, and neuronal pathways.
source: Expression profiling of murine intestinal tuft cells using a transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member 5 (Trpm5)-GFP reporter (Bezençon et al., 2008) suggested that tuft cells have a role in chemosensory, immune, and neuronal pathways, the latter two of which are not typically associated with epithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Tuft cells in the gastrointestinal tract are important for initiating Type 2 immunity and epithelial tissue remodeling.
source: In major paradigm-building work, tuft cells were recently identified in the gastrointestinal tract as being important for initiating Type 2 immunity and epithelial tissue remodeling (Gerbe et al., 2016; Howitt et al., 2016; von Moltke et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tuft cells are the sole producers of interleukin (IL)-25, needed to activate the ILC2-circuit required for promoting anti-parasitic immune responses.
source: In addition, tuft cells were found to be the sole producers of interleukin (IL)-25, needed to activate the ILC2-circuit required for promoting anti-parasitic immune responses (Gerbe et al., 2016; Howitt et al., 2016; von Moltke et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tuft cell expansion in the gastrointestinal tract requires IL-25 and IL-4ra signaling.
source: It was also determined that tuft cell expansion in the gastrointestinal tract requires this Type 2 immune response, specifically IL-25 and IL-4ra signaling (Gerbe et al., 2016; Howitt et al., 2016; von Moltke et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tuft cell specification depends on the master transcription factor POU domain, class 2, transcription factor 3 (Pou2F3).
source: Additionally, tuft cell specification depends on the master transcription factor POU domain, class 2, transcription factor 3 (Pou2F3) (Gerbe et al., 2016; Ohmoto et al., 2013; Yamaguchi et al., 2014; Yamashita et al., 2017), also required for the development of type II/bitter taste bud cells (Matsumoto et al., 2011), to which tuft cells are very closely related.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tuft cell expansion has been demonstrated to occur after severe SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans.
source: Importantly, tuft cell expansion has recently been demonstrated to occur after severe SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans as well (Melms et al., 2021), possibly contributing to 'long COVID' pulmonary symptoms, a significant and growing public health concern.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Tuft cell expansion after SARS-CoV-2 infection may contribute to 'long COVID' pulmonary symptoms.
source: Importantly, tuft cell expansion has recently been demonstrated to occur after severe SARS-CoV-2 infection in humans as well (Melms et al., 2021), possibly contributing to 'long COVID' pulmonary symptoms, a significant and growing public health concern.
evidence: Speculative statement based on correlation between tuft cell expansion and long COVID symptoms.

claim: The presence of tuft cells in dysplastic regions of the lung correlated with features of a chronic Type 2 immune response.
source: In addition, the presence of tuft cells in dysplastic regions of the lung correlated with features of a chronic Type 2 immune response, such as increased eosinophilia, goblet cell hyperplasia, and IL-13 long after viral clearance (Keeler et al., 2018; Rane et al., 2019), raising potential concern for their possible contribution to post-viral reactive airway disease and/or chronic inflammation.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Bulk RNA-Seq revealed a transcriptomic signature of post-influenza lung tuft cells highly conserved with both intestinal and tracheal tuft cells.
source: Bulk RNA-Seq (Figure 1D–E) revealed a transcriptomic signature highly conserved with both intestinal and tracheal tuft cells (Nadjsombati et al., 2018), including enrichment in key tuft cell markers including Trpm5, Sox9, and Dclk1 (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1D-E and comparison with published data.

claim: 898 genes were differentially expressed between purified tuft cells and the remaining lung epithelium.
source: In total, 898 genes were differentially expressed between purified tuft cells and the remaining lung epithelium (adjusted p-value <0.05).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Post-influenza lung tuft cells express Chat and Plcb2 at reduced levels compared to tracheal tuft cells.
source: An apparent distinction is reduced expression of Chat and Plcb2 by post-influenza lung tuft cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of bulk RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single-cell RNA-Seq analysis revealed three to five populations of tuft cells depending upon clustering variables.
source: Among these, we observed three to five populations of cells depending upon clustering variables (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: One population of tuft cells (cluster 2) co-expressed basal cell markers Krt5 and Trp63, suggesting these were basal cells early in their differentiation toward tuft cells.
source: One of these populations (cluster 2) co-expressed basal cell markers Krt5 and Trp63, suggesting that these were basal cells very early in their differentiation toward tuft cells, in agreement with our earlier demonstration that all post-IAV tuft cells are derived from intrapulmonary p63+ basal-like cells (Rane et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-Seq data and prior published work.

claim: 90% of Dclk1+ cells were labeled by Krt5-CreERT2 lineage tracing in the alveoli.
source: To further confirm that tuft cells are derived from basal-like cells after flu, we performed lineage tracing using Krt5-CreERT2 and found that 90% of Dclk1+ cells were labeled in the alveoli, with tdTomato signal clearly visible in tuft cell nuclei (Figure 2E, n=323 Dclk1+ cells).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Post-influenza lung tuft cells include a small subpopulation of 'Tuft-1' cells uniquely expressing known Tuft-1 genes.
source: Utilizing published gene sets for these two tuft cell subtypes, we performed gene module enrichment in Seurat, revealing a small subpopulation of 'Tuft-1' cells uniquely expressing known Tuft-1 genes, and a larger subpopulation of 'Tuft-2' cells, whose gene expression is relatively broad, but is expressed higher in this subpopulation than in 'Tuft-1' subpopulation (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by gene module enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Post-influenza lung tuft cells include a larger subpopulation of 'Tuft-2' cells.
source: Utilizing published gene sets for these two tuft cell subtypes, we performed gene module enrichment in Seurat, revealing a small subpopulation of 'Tuft-1' cells uniquely expressing known Tuft-1 genes, and a larger subpopulation of 'Tuft-2' cells, whose gene expression is relatively broad, but is expressed higher in this subpopulation than in 'Tuft-1' subpopulation (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by gene module enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 20% of Trpm5-GFP+ cells express Gnb3 in situ.
source: To corroborate these as distinct identities in vivo, we performed immunostaining for 'Tuft-1' marker Gnb3 in Trpm5-GFP reporter mice, observing distinct Gnb3 expression in approximately 20% of Trpm5-GFP+ cells in situ (Figure 2F), though we did not observe any preferential localization of Gnb3+ cells.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Pou2f3-/- mice entirely failed to develop lung tuft cells after influenza infection.
source: As expected, Pou2f3-/- mice entirely failed to develop lung tuft cells (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Trpm5-/- mice, tuft cells still differentiate after IAV injury.
source: In Trpm5-/- mice, tuft cells still differentiate after IAV injury, and we did not observe a significant change in tuft cell number at 25 days post injury (Figure 3E–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3E-G and supplements.

claim: No difference in total numbers of tuft cells was observed in Il4ra-/- animals after influenza infection.
source: Though we anticipated a recapitulation of the circuit found in the small intestine, we observed no difference in total numbers of tuft cells in either Il4ra-/- (Figure 3I–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C) or Il25-/- animals (Figure 3M–O).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3I-K and supplements.

claim: No difference in total numbers of tuft cells was observed in Il25-/- animals after influenza infection.
source: Though we anticipated a recapitulation of the circuit found in the small intestine, we observed no difference in total numbers of tuft cells in either Il4ra-/- (Figure 3I–K, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C) or Il25-/- animals (Figure 3M–O).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3M-O.

claim: Using an inducible, ubiquitously expressed Cre and floxed Il4ra allele resulted in no significant difference in tuft cell numbers compared with controls.
source: An alternative strategy to eliminate IL-4ra signaling, using an inducible, ubiquitously expressed Cre and floxed ll4ra allele, again resulted in no significant difference in tuft cell numbers compared with controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Il4, Il5, or Il13 levels were not significantly increased at 12, 21, or 51 days post infection when tuft cells are present in the lung.
source: Consistent with independence from Type 2 cytokines, in normal mice following infection, we did not observe significantly increased levels of Il4, Il5, or Il13, at timepoints when tuft cells are present in the lung – 12, 21, or 51 days post infection, although we did observe significant induction of Type 2 cytokines at earlier timepoints (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The loss of tuft cells in Pou2f3-/- mice had no effect on viral clearance.
source: Additionally, we found that the loss of tuft cells in the Pou2f3-/- mice had no effect on viral clearance (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B), in line with the timing that flu-induced tuft cells arise at timepoints well after viral clearance (Rane et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B and prior published work.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in overall Krt5+ area in Pou2f3-/- mutant compared to control after influenza infection.
source: There was also no statistically significant difference of overall Krt5+ area in Pou2f3-/- mutant where tuft cells are not present compared to control (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No significant difference was detected in the percent of proliferating (Ki67+) alveolar Krt5+ basal-like cells at 14 or 25 days post infection in Pou2f3-/- mice.
source: Consistently, we did not detect a significant difference in the percent of proliferating (Ki67+) alveolar Krt5+ basal-like cells at 14 or 25 days post infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 5C-D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5C-D.

claim: Post-injury tuft cells and Th2 immune signals (IL-4, IL-13, and IL-25) are apparently dispensable for the formation of Krt5+ cells in injured lungs.
source: While we cannot rule out differences in the behavior of other reparative cells, these findings indicate that post-injury tuft cells and Th2 immune signals (at least IL-4, IL-13, and IL-25) are apparently dispensable for the formation of Krt5+ cells in injured lungs.
evidence: Inference based on data showing no significant difference in Krt5+ area in various knockout mice.

claim: Type I (α/β) interferon signaling is dispensable for the development of post-injury tuft cells.
source: Type I (α/β) and type III (λ) interferon signaling are dispensable for the development of post-injury tuft cells
evidence: Supported by data in Ifnar-/- mice showing no significant difference in tuft cell numbers (Figure 4D-F).

claim: Type III (λ) interferon signaling is dispensable for the development of post-injury tuft cells.
source: Type I (α/β) and type III (λ) interferon signaling are dispensable for the development of post-injury tuft cells
evidence: Supported by data in Il28r-/- mice showing no significant difference in tuft cell numbers (Figure 4A-C).

claim: Type I (α/β) and type III (λ) interferons are highly expressed following influenza infection.
source: Type I (α/β) and type III (λ) interferons are highly expressed following influenza infection (Killip et al., 2015) and are crucial components of the innate anti-viral response (Pardy et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Interferons are crucial components of the innate anti-viral response.
source: Type I (α/β) and type III (λ) interferons are highly expressed following influenza infection (Killip et al., 2015) and are crucial components of the innate anti-viral response (Pardy et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The action of type III interferon is restricted to the epithelium.
source: As interferons play a crucial role early in flu infection and the action of type III interferon is restricted to the epithelium (Killip et al., 2015), we assessed whether they play a role in tuft cell development post IAV infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: IFNAR-deficient mice have increased mortality when infected with flu.
source: Since IFNAR-deficient mice have been shown to have increased mortality when infected with flu (Arimori et al., 2013; Killip et al., 2015; Seo et al., 2011), we infected Ifnar1- and Il28r-deficient mice with a lower dose of PR8 than their BL/6 controls.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tuft cells (Dclk1+) were identified within Krt5+ patches in the lungs of bleomycin-treated mice.
source: We identified tuft cells (Dclk1+) within Krt5+ patches in the lungs of bleomycin-treated mice by immunostaining, albeit sparser than in IAV-infected mice (Figure 4G, n=3 mice).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Tuft cell development can occur independently of infection and is a result of lung injury.
source: These data demonstrated that tuft cell development can occur independently of infection and is a result of lung injury.
evidence: Inference based on observation of tuft cells in bleomycin injury model.

claim: Amplification of tuft cells in the intestine promotes goblet cell metaplasia through Th2 cytokines.
source: Amplification of tuft cells in the intestine promotes goblet cell metaplasia through Th2 cytokines (Gerbe et al., 2016; von Moltke et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In Pou2f3-/-, Trpm5-/-, and Il4ra-/- animals, the percent of Agr2+ area within Krt5+ area was not significantly different from controls following influenza infection.
source: We found that in Pou2f3-/-, Trpm5-/-, and Il4ra-/- animals, the percent of Agr2+ area within Krt5+ area was not significantly different from controls following influenza infection (Figure 5A–I).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5A-I.

claim: Muc5b immunostaining in damaged regions of lung did not differ between Pou2f3-/- or Il4ra-/- lungs 25 days post infection.
source: Consistent with this, Muc5b immunostaining in damaged regions of lung did not differ between Pou2f3-/- or Il4ra-/- lungs 25 days post infection (Figure 5J–M).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5J-M.

claim: No significant difference was observed in relative expression of goblet cell markers when normalizing to Actb or to Krt5 in Pou2f3-/- animals 51 days post infection.
source: In order to quantify mucus metaplasia in whole lungs of control and Pou2f3-/- animals, we analyzed gene expression of goblet cell markers, Foxa3, Agr2, Muc5ac, and Muc5b, 51 days post infection. We did not observe a significant difference in relative expression of goblet cell markers when normalizing to Actb or to Krt5 as a marker of tissue damage (Figure 5N).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: Basal-like cells are rarely observed to act as progenitors for AT1s or AT2s after IAV injury.
source: After IAV injury, basal-like cells are rarely observed to act as progenitors for AT1s or AT2s, though they do so at a higher frequency after bleomycin injury as indicated by lineage tracing with Krt5-creERT2 labeling AT2s (Vaughan et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Basal-like cells act as progenitors for AT2s at a higher frequency after bleomycin injury than after IAV injury.
source: After IAV injury, basal-like cells are rarely observed to act as progenitors for AT1s or AT2s, though they do so at a higher frequency after bleomycin injury as indicated by lineage tracing with Krt5-creERT2 labeling AT2s (Vaughan et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: No overlap of Krt5 and SPC staining was observed in either Pou2f3-/- or control lungs at 25 days after infection.
source: To address if a relatively minor population of Krt5+ cells may be converting to AT2s, we double stained for Krt5 and the AT2 cell marker SPC+ in Pou2f3-/- and control lungs at 25 days after infection to label cells in the process of conversion (Figure 6A). We did not observe any overlap of staining in either Pou2f3-/- or control lungs.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: No appreciable conversion of Krt5+ precursors into AT2 (SPC+) cells was observed in the presence or absence of tuft cells.
source: To more rigorously trace possible conversion, we bred Pou2f3-/- mice to Krt5-CreERT2 fate mapping mice to lineage trace Krt5+ cells and assess whether any increased plasticity may occur in the absence of tuft cells (Figure 6B). Unlike tuft cells, which could be lineage traced from Krt5+ precursors, we did not observe any appreciable conversion of Krt5+ precursors into AT2 (SPC+) cells in the presence or absence of tuft cells (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Ectopic lung tuft cells do not appear to play an important role in restricting Krt5+ epithelial cell plasticity.
source: Taken together, while ectopic lung tuft cells likely possess as-of-yet undiscovered function in post-IAV lungs, it does not appear that they play an important role in restricting Krt5+ epithelial cell plasticity, nor are they responsible for the inability of Krt5+ cells to efficiently differentiate into more regionally appropriate alveolar cell types.
evidence: Inference based on data showing no difference in Krt5+ to AT2 conversion in presence or absence of tuft cells.

claim: Ectopic lung tuft cells are not responsible for the inability of Krt5+ cells to efficiently differentiate into more regionally appropriate alveolar cell types.
source: Taken together, while ectopic lung tuft cells likely possess as-of-yet undiscovered function in post-IAV lungs, it does not appear that they play an important role in restricting Krt5+ epithelial cell plasticity, nor are they responsible for the inability of Krt5+ cells to efficiently differentiate into more regionally appropriate alveolar cell types.
evidence: Inference based on data showing no difference in Krt5+ to AT2 conversion in presence or absence of tuft cells.

claim: Single-cell RNA-Seq data revealed heterogeneity among influenza-induced lung tuft cells, including a 'basal/tuft' hybrid cluster.
source: Our single-cell RNA-Seq data revealed heterogeneity among these lung tuft cells, including a 'basal/tuft' hybrid cluster, consistent with lineage tracing Dclk1+ tuft cells from p63+/Krt5+ basal progenitors, and 'Tuft-1' and 'Tuft-2' clusters, distinct subtypes enriched for genes related to sensory functions and eicosanoid synthesis, respectively.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Single-cell RNA-Seq data revealed 'Tuft-1' and 'Tuft-2' clusters, distinct subtypes enriched for genes related to sensory functions and eicosanoid synthesis, respectively.
source: Our single-cell RNA-Seq data revealed heterogeneity among these lung tuft cells, including a 'basal/tuft' hybrid cluster, consistent with lineage tracing Dclk1+ tuft cells from p63+/Krt5+ basal progenitors, and 'Tuft-1' and 'Tuft-2' clusters, distinct subtypes enriched for genes related to sensory functions and eicosanoid synthesis, respectively.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-Seq data and gene module enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The formation of lung tuft cells depends on the cell type-defining transcription factor gene Pou2f3.
source: Similar to tuft cells in the intestine, we found that the formation of lung tuft cells depends on the cell type-defining transcription factor gene Pou2f3.
evidence: Supported by data showing absence of tuft cells in Pou2f3-/- mice (Figure 3A-C).

claim: Unlike intestinal tuft cells which are dependent on Th2 cytokines for their amplification, lung tuft cells arise in similar numbers in Il25-/- or Il4ra-/- mutants compared to controls following infection.
source: However, despite this shared dependence and common gene expression signatures, we identified major differences in the behavior of lung tuft cells compared to their intestinal counterpart. Unlike intestinal tuft cells which are dependent on Th2 cytokines for their amplification, lung tuft cells arise in similar numbers in Il25-/- or Il4ra-/- mutants compared to controls following infection.
evidence: Supported by data in Il25-/- and Il4ra-/- mice showing no significant difference in tuft cell numbers (Figure 3I-O).

claim: Lung tuft cells appear dispensable for the formation of Krt5+ cells from p63+ basal-like cells.
source: Moreover, while intestinal tuft cells strongly influence the growth and differentiation of surrounding epithelial cells in infectious/inflammatory settings, lung tuft cells appear dispensable for the formation of Krt5+ cells from p63+ basal-like cells, their migration into damaged alveoli, and goblet cell metaplasia.
evidence: Supported by data showing no significant difference in Krt5+ area in Pou2f3-/- mice (Figure 3A-D).

claim: Lung tuft cells appear dispensable for goblet cell metaplasia.
source: Moreover, while intestinal tuft cells strongly influence the growth and differentiation of surrounding epithelial cells in infectious/inflammatory settings, lung tuft cells appear dispensable for the formation of Krt5+ cells from p63+ basal-like cells, their migration into damaged alveoli, and goblet cell metaplasia.
evidence: Supported by data showing no significant difference in goblet cell markers in Pou2f3-/- mice (Figure 5A-N).

claim: Experiments in Pou2f3-/- and Il4ra-/- mice were performed entirely independently in separate vivariums, yet observed the same conclusions.
source: The interpretations of experimental outcomes in Pou2f3-/- and Il4ra-/- mice are further strengthened by the fact that our two groups performed these experiments entirely independently in separate vivariums, yet observed the same conclusions, arguing against a prominent role for differing housing environments in directing development and function of ectopic tuft cells.
evidence: Statement about experimental design and reproducibility.

claim: In the trachea, i.p. administration of IL-13 was found to increase tuft cell numbers.
source: In the trachea, i.p. administration of IL-13 was found to increase tuft cell numbers (Ualiyeva et al., 2021), and baseline tuft cell numbers were reduced in Stat6-/- mice, with blunted response to Th2 signals (Bankova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Baseline tuft cell numbers were reduced in Stat6-/- mice, with blunted response to Th2 signals.
source: In the trachea, i.p. administration of IL-13 was found to increase tuft cell numbers (Ualiyeva et al., 2021), and baseline tuft cell numbers were reduced in Stat6-/- mice, with blunted response to Th2 signals (Bankova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: IL-13 promotes prostaglandin E2 generation in upper airway tuft cells, in turn promoting CFTR-mediated mucocilliary transport.
source: Moreover, IL-13 promotes prostaglandin E2 generation in upper airway tuft cells, in turn promoting CFTR-mediated mucocilliary transport (Kotas et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: IL-13 plays no role in the development of tuft cells after injury and remodeling in distal lung.
source: In contrast to these findings which suggest that IL-13 signaling influences upper airway tuft cell differentiation, our data in distal lung indicate that IL-13 plays no role in the development of tuft cells after injury and remodeling, a somewhat surprising discrepancy given the cellular similarity between the dysplastic, 'bronchiolized' Krt5+ regions and tracheal epithelium.
evidence: Inference based on data showing no difference in tuft cell numbers in Il4ra-/- mice, which lack IL-13 signaling.

claim: Airway hyperreactivity and airway mucus production after IAV infection are partially attenuated in Il13 knockout mice.
source: Other aspects of lung remodeling after IAV infection, including airway hyperreactivity and airway mucus production, are partially attenuated in Il13 knockout mice (Keeler et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mucus is not significantly reduced within the most severely damaged regions of the distal lung in Il13 knockout mice.
source: However, mucus is not significantly reduced within the most severely damaged regions of the distal lung (Keeler et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Some outcomes of pathologic lung remodeling after IAV infection are dependent on Type 2 cytokines, while others are independent.
source: Our results build upon these findings and cumulatively indicate that while some outcomes of pathologic lung remodeling after IAV infection are dependent on Type 2 cytokines, others are independent.
evidence: Inference based on data showing differential effects of Type 2 cytokine signaling on different aspects of lung remodeling.

claim: In the trachea, tuft cell differentiation following challenge with the allergen Alternaria is dependent on leukotriene signaling.
source: In the trachea, tuft cell differentiation following challenge with the allergen Alternaria is dependent on leukotriene signaling, and leukotriene LTE4 administration is sufficient to increase tuft cells (Bankova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Leukotriene LTE4 administration is sufficient to increase tuft cells in the trachea.
source: In the trachea, tuft cell differentiation following challenge with the allergen Alternaria is dependent on leukotriene signaling, and leukotriene LTE4 administration is sufficient to increase tuft cells (Bankova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The increase in tuft cells by leukotriene signaling is independent of Stat6, suggestive of a distinct pathway from that of the Th2 cytokines.
source: This increase is independent of Stat6, suggestive of a distinct pathway from that of the Th2 cytokines (Bankova et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In the trachea, tuft cell-produced inflammatory mediators IL-25 and LTC4 synergize with each other to promote Type 2 inflammation, including eosinophil recruitment and ILC2 proliferation.
source: In the trachea, these tuft cell-produced inflammatory mediators synergize with each other to promote Type 2 inflammation, including eosinophil recruitment and ILC2 proliferation (Ualiyeva et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In the small intestine, tuft cell-produced leukotrienes are important for helminth clearance but dispensable for Th2 responses to protist infection.
source: In the small intestine, while tuft cell-produced leukotrienes are important for helminth clearance, they are dispensable for Th2 responses to protist infection (McGinty et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In both the trachea and the small intestine, the sensory function of existing tuft cells serves as a starting point in a positive feedback loop triggering immune activation and tuft cell hyperplasia.
source: In both the trachea and the small intestine, the sensory function of existing tuft cells serves as a starting point in a positive feedback loop triggering immune activation and tuft cell hyperplasia.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from published literature.

claim: Tuft cells are not present in quiescent lung.
source: In comparison, tuft cells are not present in quiescent lung.
evidence: Based on prior observations and established knowledge.

claim: Following IAV infection, tuft cells arise from basal-like cells.
source: Following IAV infection, they arise from basal-like cells.
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 2E and prior published work.

claim: The apparent increased density of tuft cells after IAV infection compared to bleomycin injury suggests that heightened immune signaling after viral infection may play a role in promoting tuft cell formation.
source: The apparent increased density of tuft cells after IAV infection compared to bleomycin injury also suggest that heightened immune signaling after viral infection may play a role in promoting tuft cell formation.
evidence: Speculative inference based on comparison of tuft cell density in different injury models.

claim: Based on RNA-Seq of purified tuft cells from multiple tissues, tuft cells across many tissues produce thymic stromal lymphopoietin, prostaglandins, and acetylcholine.
source: Based on RNA-Seq of purified tuft cells from multiple tissues (Nadjsombati et al., 2018), in addition to IL-25 and leukotrienes, tuft cells across many tissues also produce thymic stromal lymphopoietin, prostaglandins (DelGiorno et al., 2020), and acetylcholine.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most ligands and proteins that produce them are expressed by damage-induced tuft cells in the lung, though reduced ChAT expression is noted in post-IAV tuft cells compared to trachea tuft cells.
source: Most of these ligands and proteins that produce them are also expressed by damage-induced tuft cells in the lung, though we note reduced ChAT expression in post-IAV tuft cells compared to trachea tuft cells.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopic lung tuft cells likely possess as-of-yet undiscovered function in post-IAV lungs.
source: Taken together, while ectopic lung tuft cells likely possess as-of-yet undiscovered function in post-IAV lungs, it does not appear that they play an important role in restricting Krt5+ epithelial cell plasticity, nor are they responsible for the inability of Krt5+ cells to efficiently differentiate into more regionally appropriate alveolar cell types.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the dramatic appearance of tuft cells despite lack of identified function.

claim: The appearance of tuft cells within the heavily injured regions is dramatic.
source: The appearance of tuft cells within the heavily injured regions is dramatic, reinforcing the need for future studies to define discrete functions of these cells in pulmonary physiology/pathophysiology.
evidence: Based on immunostaining data showing abundant tuft cells in injured regions.
